lesson.title: AWS S3: ownership encryption lifecycle and checksums
lesson.why: An object can be encrypted yet publicly readable, correctly owned yet corrupted before upload, or cheaply stored but expensive to retrieve. These are separate design questions.
lesson.what: Evaluate object ownership, authorization guardrails, encryption, retention, and integrity for a fictional report archive without uploading data.

concepts.name: Ownership is not public-access prevention
concepts.body: Bucket owner enforced Object Ownership disables ACLs and makes the bucket owner own uploaded objects. Block Public Access separately constrains public policies and ACL behavior. Keeping ACLs disabled does not itself prevent an overly permissive bucket policy from exposing data.

concepts.name: Encryption needs authorization
concepts.body: S3 encrypts new objects at rest by default, but encryption does not replace access controls. SSE-KMS adds key-policy and KMS-permission considerations, quotas, and possible request charges. An authorized object request can still fail because access to the encryption key is missing.

concepts.name: Lifecycle follows retention intent
concepts.body: Lifecycle rules can transition objects and expire eligible versions. Versioned buckets need separate treatment of current versions, noncurrent versions, and delete markers. Archive retrieval latency, minimum storage duration, request fees, and retained old versions can outweigh apparent storage savings.

concepts.name: ETags are not universal hashes
concepts.body: An ETag is not reliably a whole-object MD5 checksum: multipart uploads and some encryption paths differ. Use documented checksum algorithms and the correct full-object or composite interpretation. Compare a trusted source checksum with the retrieved bytes; a checksum cannot authenticate an untrusted publisher by itself.

e2e: Classify the reports by confidentiality, retention, and required retrieval time.
Choose ownership and public-access guardrails independently, then scope access policies.
Select encryption and document who can use the key during normal access and recovery.
Model lifecycle transitions for every object version and expected retrieval pattern.
Verify integrity with supported checksum semantics and rehearse restoration before relying on archives.

tasks.name: Separate four controls
steps: Create rows for ownership, Block Public Access, encryption, and checksums.
Assign respectively ACL ownership behavior, public exposure limits, data-at-rest protection, and accidental-change detection. Explain why none alone answers all four requirements.

tasks.name: Verify a local checksum
tasks.goal: Run a harmless deterministic integrity example.
steps: Run locally: python -c "import hashlib; print(hashlib.sha256(b'abc').hexdigest())".

Expected output: ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad. Change the bytes to b'abd' and observe a different digest; this does not prove S3 authorization or multipart checksum handling.

tasks.name: Account for retained versions
steps: Assume ten 2-GB reports each retain three full versions. Expected stored data before overhead is 10 x 2 x 3 = 60 GB, not 20 GB.
Explain that deleting current versions in a versioned bucket need not erase older billable versions.

tasks.name: Design recovery evidence
steps: A report is needed within five minutes during an audit. Reject a retrieval option whose documented delay cannot meet that requirement.
Write checks for restored bytes, key access, and version identity. Use only synthetic reports in any later approved test.

key_terms: Object Ownership: bucket setting governing ownership and ACL use.
BPA: Block Public Access guardrails.
SSE-KMS: server-side encryption using KMS keys.
Noncurrent version: an older retained object version.
Checksum: value computed to detect data changes.
lesson.safety: No uploads are required. Storage, requests, KMS, retrieval, and early-deletion charges may apply in real accounts. Never test public access using sensitive reports.
cleanup: The hash command creates no files.
Discard synthetic retention notes; future tests must inspect noncurrent versions and incomplete multipart uploads before claiming cleanup.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an encrypted S3 archive uses bucket-owner-enforced ownership. What additional evidence would you request before calling it protected?
interview_points: Inspect public-access settings and policies.
Check KMS recovery access if used.
Review version retention and retrieval objectives.
Validate checksums without assuming ETag equals MD5.

aws-data/aws-s3-ownership-encryption-lif.core: S3 ownership, public-access blocking, encryption, lifecycle, and integrity are independent controls. Evaluate all object versions and retrieval costs. Use supported checksums rather than treating every ETag as a whole-object MD5.

storyboard.title: An archive restore needs both access and integrity
storyboard.objective: Connect upload protection, denied key access, and verified recovery.

scenes.title: Read retained data
scenes.caption: The requested version remains available.
scenes.narration: The auditor selects a retained report version and requests it through the approved access path rather than public sharing.

scenes.title: Key access is missing
scenes.caption: Object permission alone is insufficient for SSE-KMS.
scenes.narration: The encryption-key authorization fails, so an otherwise permitted object read cannot supply the report to the auditor.

scenes.title: Recover and verify
scenes.caption: Authorized recovery also checks content integrity.
scenes.narration: After approved key-policy repair, the reader retrieves the exact version and compares its checksum using the documented algorithm.

lesson.title: AWS RDS: Multi-AZ replicas backup and recovery
lesson.why: Availability, read scaling, and recovery from accidental deletion require different mechanisms. Calling every secondary database a replica hides important operational differences.
lesson.what: Choose between traditional Multi-AZ DB instances, Multi-AZ DB clusters, asynchronous read replicas, and point-in-time recovery using explicit workload objectives.

concepts.name: Traditional standby is not readable
concepts.body: A traditional Multi-AZ DB instance deployment synchronously maintains a standby in another zone for failover. That standby does not serve application reads. It improves availability but does not provide read scaling, and failover still requires clients to reconnect appropriately.

concepts.name: Multi-AZ clusters are different
concepts.body: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readable instances across three zones for supported engines and configurations. This is not the same topology as the single-standby deployment, nor should its behavior be generalized to every RDS engine.

concepts.name: Read replicas address a separate need
concepts.body: Read replicas ordinarily use asynchronous replication and may lag their source. They can offload suitable reads, but immediate read-after-write requirements may need the writer. Promotion changes topology and endpoints; replication alone does not provide an independent history of good data.

concepts.name: Backups recover earlier state
concepts.body: Automated backups and transaction logs support recovery within the configured retention and available restore window. Restoring normally creates a new database rather than rewinding the running one. A replicated accidental deletion can reach secondaries, so restore rehearsals complement high availability.

e2e: Specify outage tolerance, acceptable data loss, read freshness, and engine requirements.
Choose availability topology separately from read-scaling topology.
Configure retention and record the latest restorable-time concept in the recovery plan.
Plan connection retry and endpoint handling for failover and for restoration.
Rehearse recovery into an isolated destination and validate data before redirecting clients.

tasks.name: Match mechanisms
tasks.goal: Choose by requirement instead of name.
steps: Map zonal writer failure, high reporting load, and an accidental table deletion to candidate mechanisms.
Expected choices are Multi-AZ availability, a suitable read replica or readable cluster member, and backup/PITR respectively; explain why no single label solves all three.

tasks.name: Calculate an RPO gap
steps: Suppose an incident occurs at 14:10 and the latest usable restore point is 14:07. The potential time gap is three minutes.
If the objective allows only one minute, this evidence fails the objective. Do not infer exact lost rows without transaction records.

tasks.name: Route freshness-sensitive reads
steps: An order write succeeds, then a replica still shows the previous state. Route the immediate confirmation to an appropriate strongly current source.
Keep analytics on the replica only if its freshness requirement tolerates measured lag; do not call asynchronous replication synchronous.

tasks.name: Draft a restore cutover
steps: List isolated restore, schema and row checks, secret/connectivity checks, controlled client cutover, and rollback to the retained source where valid.
The paper rehearsal cannot establish actual failover duration, RPO, or IAM behavior.

key_terms: Standby: failover instance not serving reads in traditional Multi-AZ.
Read replica: asynchronously updated read-serving copy.
PITR: point-in-time recovery within an available window.
RPO: acceptable data-loss window.
RTO: target time to restore useful service.
lesson.safety: Do not create databases or trigger failover. Replicas, backups, restored instances, I/O, and transfer can add charges; production restore tests require isolation and approval.
cleanup: A future test must remove its restored instance only after evidence review and explicitly handle retained snapshots.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, someone proposes a traditional Multi-AZ standby for reporting and as protection against accidental DELETE. What would you correct?
interview_points: The traditional standby is not readable.
Readable Multi-AZ clusters are a distinct deployment option.
Replicated deletion requires historical recovery, not merely failover.
Test restore and connection behavior against RPO/RTO.

aws-data/aws-rds-multi-az-replicas-backu.core: Traditional RDS Multi-AZ standby provides failover, not reads. Multi-AZ DB clusters have readable members. Asynchronous replicas can lag, while backups/PITR recover historical state into a new destination.

storyboard.title: Failover cannot undo a replicated deletion
storyboard.objective: Separate availability replicas from historical recovery.

scenes.title: Healthy replication
scenes.caption: The standby tracks committed primary changes.
scenes.narration: Normal writes are replicated for availability, while clients read and write through the primary rather than the traditional standby.

scenes.title: Bad deletion propagates
scenes.caption: Availability is not historical protection.
scenes.narration: An authorized but mistaken deletion is a valid database change, so replication does not preserve an untouched standby copy.

scenes.title: Restore earlier state
scenes.caption: Validate a separate recovery destination.
scenes.narration: Operators restore a suitable earlier point into isolation, verify its contents, and plan client cutover without destroying incident evidence.

lesson.title: AWS Aurora architecture and failover
lesson.why: Aurora separates compute from distributed storage, but resilient storage does not make one writer process immortal. Client reconnection and readable capacity remain part of availability design.
lesson.what: Trace a regional Aurora cluster through write, read, failure, and promotion. Keep regional availability distinct from cross-region disaster recovery and engine-specific behavior.

concepts.name: Storage and compute have different jobs
concepts.body: Aurora maintains multiple storage copies across Availability Zones, independently of the number of compute instances. Writer and reader instances access a shared cluster volume. Adding a reader adds database compute capacity; it does not create an entirely separate logical backup of the data.

concepts.name: Endpoints express roles
concepts.body: The cluster writer endpoint tracks the current writer. The reader endpoint distributes new reader connections across eligible readers rather than balancing every SQL query individually. Long-lived connection pools can concentrate work, and stale DNS or cached connections can delay recovery.

concepts.name: Failover promotes eligible compute
concepts.body: When a writer fails, Aurora can promote a suitable replica, with promotion tiers and availability influencing selection. Having ready capacity in another zone reduces dependence on creating a replacement from scratch. Applications must retry connections and transactions carefully because commit outcomes can be ambiguous.

concepts.name: Regional replicas are not global recovery
concepts.body: Aurora Global Database provides a separate cross-region architecture with replication and managed recovery workflows. Cross-region behavior, engine support, and replication mode must be checked explicitly. Neither regional shared storage nor a global secondary substitutes for backups against logical corruption.

e2e: Place writer and suitable reader compute across zones with documented promotion priorities.
Send writes to the writer endpoint and only freshness-tolerant reads to readers.
Observe replica lag, connection pools, and storage/compute saturation independently.
On writer failure, refresh connections and use bounded transaction retries with idempotency.
Validate the promoted writer and separately rehearse historical and cross-region recovery requirements.

tasks.name: Draw separate planes
tasks.goal: Distinguish compute replicas from storage copies.
steps: Sketch one writer and two readers above a shared multi-zone cluster volume.
Label promotion candidates and explain why deleting a table is not safely undone by connecting to another reader.

tasks.name: Model reader connections
steps: Assume twelve long-lived connections are initially distributed six to each of two readers. Add a third reader without reopening any connections.
Expected existing distribution remains 6, 6, 0 in this simplified model. New connections may use the reader endpoint, but old connections do not teleport between instances.

tasks.name: Trace an ambiguous commit
steps: A client submits an order transaction and loses its connection before receiving confirmation.
Record the order's stable identifier, reconnect through the writer endpoint, and check committed state before retrying. A network error alone does not prove rollback.

tasks.name: Review a recovery proposal
steps: A proposal has durable multi-zone storage but only one compute instance and no restore exercise.
Request ready failover compute where required, backup validation, and a separate regional-outage plan. Offline diagrams do not prove actual failover timing.

key_terms: Cluster volume: shared distributed Aurora storage.
Writer endpoint: endpoint tracking the writable instance.
Reader endpoint: connection distributor for eligible readers.
Promotion tier: preference influencing failover selection.
Ambiguous commit: unknown transaction outcome after connection loss.
lesson.safety: No cluster is created. Reader instances, I/O, backups, global replication, and proxy services can add cost. Failover drills require approval and synthetic transactions.
cleanup: Future approved drills must remove added test readers and review retained snapshots and logs.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, Aurora storage is healthy after a writer failure but clients still error. What layers would you investigate?
interview_points: Check promotion and availability of reader compute.
Inspect endpoint DNS and connection-pool refresh.
Handle ambiguous transactions with idempotent retries.
Measure useful application recovery, not storage health alone.

aws-data/aws-aurora-architecture-and-fai.core: Aurora separates shared multi-zone storage from writer and reader compute. Writer failover still needs eligible capacity and client reconnection. Reader endpoints balance connections, while backups and cross-region recovery solve different risks.

storyboard.title: Aurora promotes a reader after writer failure

scenes.title: Normal writes
scenes.caption: A pooled connection targets the current writer.
scenes.narration: The application commits work through the writer endpoint while another-zone reader remains available as a promotion candidate.

scenes.title: Writer becomes unavailable
scenes.caption: Existing connections may fail despite durable storage.
scenes.narration: The writer process fails, breaking active sessions; storage durability alone cannot complete the application's next database request.

scenes.title: Refresh and verify
scenes.caption: Reconnection follows promotion and endpoint changes.
scenes.narration: The reader is promoted, the pool establishes new writer connections, and the application resolves ambiguous operations before retrying.

lesson.title: AWS DynamoDB partitioning consistency and capacity
lesson.why: A table with ample aggregate capacity can still suffer a hot key. Efficient DynamoDB design begins with access patterns, item sizes, and correctness requirements.
lesson.what: Model partition and sort keys, consistency, conditional writes, and capacity units on synthetic order data. Do not infer real throughput from an offline dictionary.

concepts.name: Keys shape distribution and queries
concepts.body: The partition key determines placement; a sort key groups and orders related items within that key. Query targets a partition-key value, whereas Scan examines broad data. A single popular key can concentrate load despite many cold keys and apparently low overall utilization.

concepts.name: Read consistency varies by surface
concepts.body: Tables and local secondary indexes support eventual and strongly consistent reads. Global secondary indexes and streams provide eventual reads. A strong read does not lock the item against a later writer; conditional expressions or transactions address separate concurrency requirements.

concepts.name: Capacity follows rounded item sizes
concepts.body: For ordinary nontransactional operations, writes consume units in 1-KB increments and strong reads in 4-KB increments; eventual reads use half the strong-read capacity for equivalent data. Transactions have different accounting. On-demand billing removes manual provisioning, not partition or account limits.

concepts.name: Indexes and conditions have costs
concepts.body: A global secondary index supports another access pattern but adds storage and write work and can introduce its own hot keys. Conditional writes protect invariants such as version checks. Blind retries after an uncertain result require idempotency, and filters do not make scanned bytes free.

e2e: List exact order lookup and customer-history access patterns before choosing keys.
Estimate item size and traffic distribution, including one unusually active customer.
Choose consistency per read path and conditions for concurrency-sensitive writes.
Calculate baseline capacity including indexes, transactions, and retry effects where relevant.
Monitor throttling and latency at the relevant key/index scope and revise distribution safely.

tasks.name: Design two lookups
steps: Use synthetic orders with customer_id, order_id, created_at, and total. Propose customer_id as a partition key and sortable order time plus ID as a sort key for customer history.
Identify an additional index or alternate key design for direct order-ID lookup.

tasks.name: Calculate capacity
tasks.goal: Produce an explicit offline unit estimate.
steps: For nontransactional 6-KB items at 100 reads/second, each strong read needs ceiling(6/4) = 2 units, totaling 200 read units/second; eventual reads need 100.
For 2.2-KB writes at 20/second, ceiling(2.2/1) x 20 = 60 write units/second, excluding index writes and retries.

tasks.name: Expose a hot key
steps: Assume 90% of requests target one customer while 999 customers share the rest.
Discuss sharding a hot access pattern versus application caching, including fan-out and ordering costs. Merely adding unrelated keys does not distribute that customer's requests.

tasks.name: Protect an update
steps: Two clients both read version 7. Require the update condition version = 7 and set version = 8.
Expected logical result is one successful update and one conflict requiring reread. This mock reasoning does not prove actual DynamoDB or IAM behavior.

key_terms: Partition key: attribute directing item placement.
Sort key: ordering key within a partition-key group.
GSI: asynchronously maintained alternate-key index.
Conditional write: update guarded by a predicate.
Hot key: disproportionately active partition-key value.
lesson.safety: Use only synthetic rows. Real scans, indexes, backups, streams, and replication can incur charges; do not load-test a shared table or assume on-demand means unlimited.
cleanup: Discard the synthetic order table and arithmetic.
No tables or indexes were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, one tenant is throttled while table-wide utilization is low. Why might increasing aggregate capacity be insufficient?
interview_points: Inspect traffic concentration on partition keys and indexes.
Estimate rounded item capacity and retry amplification.
Consider sharding with explicit query trade-offs.
Keep consistency and conditional-write requirements intact.

aws-data/aws-dynamodb-partitioning-consi.core: DynamoDB performance depends on key distribution and rounded item sizes, not just table totals. Tables/LSIs can use strong reads; GSIs cannot. Conditional writes solve races that fresh reads alone do not prevent.

storyboard.title: A popular customer creates a DynamoDB hot key
storyboard.objective: Connect key distribution to throttling and design recovery.

scenes.title: Normal distribution
scenes.caption: Keys receive manageable request rates.
scenes.narration: Customer requests spread across partition-key values, allowing the table's distributed storage to serve the modeled access pattern.

scenes.title: One key dominates
scenes.caption: Low table averages hide concentrated pressure.
scenes.narration: A major tenant generates most requests against one key, creating throttling that unrelated idle keys do not relieve.

scenes.title: Revise the access pattern
scenes.caption: Distribution changes require query trade-offs.
scenes.narration: Engineers evaluate sharding or caching, explicitly account for fan-out and consistency, and validate the revised pattern before rollout.

lesson.title: AWS EBS EFS and storage selection
lesson.why: Applications expect different storage interfaces. Choosing object, block, or shared-file storage incorrectly can introduce corruption, latency, or a hidden single-zone dependency.
lesson.what: Match EBS and EFS to access semantics, failure domains, throughput, and recovery needs. Compare a database volume and shared content directory without mounting cloud storage.

concepts.name: EBS is block storage
concepts.body: An EBS volume presents block devices to compatible compute within its Availability Zone. The guest filesystem or database controls layout and consistency. Ordinary single-writer filesystems must not be mounted read-write by multiple hosts merely because a specialized multi-attach option exists.

concepts.name: EFS is shared file storage
concepts.body: EFS exposes managed NFS file semantics through mount targets. Regional and One Zone storage choices have different resilience characteristics. File permissions, access points, network access, and application locking still matter; sharing a directory does not make every application safe for concurrent writers.

concepts.name: Performance has several ceilings
concepts.body: IOPS measures operation rate; throughput measures bytes per second; latency measures completion delay. Small random database I/O and large sequential files stress different limits. Instance bandwidth, volume configuration, filesystem mode, and access pattern can bottleneck before nominal storage capacity is exhausted.

concepts.name: Snapshots need application consistency
concepts.body: A storage snapshot captures a recoverable storage state, not automatically a transactionally consistent application checkpoint across every device. Coordinate database backup or quiescing requirements and restore tests. EBS snapshots can support recreating volumes elsewhere, but the original attached volume remains zonal.

e2e: Record whether the application needs blocks, shared POSIX-like files, or whole objects.
Identify concurrent writers, locking behavior, zone-loss requirements, and recovery targets.
Estimate IOPS and throughput separately using representative operation sizes.
Choose a storage configuration and backup method compatible with the application's consistency needs.
Rehearse restore and remount sequencing, then validate permissions and application data before cutover.

tasks.name: Select an interface
tasks.goal: Avoid treating storage names as interchangeable.
steps: Compare a single database expecting a block device with multiple Linux workers sharing an NFS-compatible document tree.
Investigate EBS for the first and EFS for the second, while checking database support and concurrent-write semantics explicitly.

tasks.name: Calculate throughput demand
steps: At 3,000 operations/second with 16 KiB each, modeled throughput is 48,000 KiB/second, or 46.875 MiB/second.
At 256 KiB per operation the same IOPS implies 750 MiB/second. Expected conclusion: an IOPS target alone is an incomplete specification.

tasks.name: Find a zone dependency
steps: Draw a server and EBS volume in zone A with replacement compute planned in zone B.
Explain why the existing volume cannot simply be attached across zones. Add a documented replication or snapshot-restoration strategy rather than pretending Auto Scaling moves the disk.

tasks.name: Review a backup claim
steps: A two-volume database snapshot was taken without documented consistency coordination. List transaction-log recovery and cross-volume consistency questions.
Draft isolated restore and integrity checks. This paper review proves neither actual recovery nor cloud permissions.

key_terms: Block storage: addressable storage blocks managed by a host.
NFS: network file-sharing protocol.
IOPS: storage operations per second.
Throughput: bytes transferred per unit time.
Quiesce: temporarily coordinate writes for a consistent capture.
lesson.safety: Do not create or mount volumes. Capacity, provisioned performance, throughput modes, snapshots, and transfer may be billable. Never practice filesystem formatting on an existing device.
cleanup: Future tests must inventory detached volumes, retained snapshots, mount targets, and application data before deletion.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a design promises cross-zone database failover by attaching the same EBS volume to a replacement server. What is missing?
interview_points: EBS attachment is constrained by Availability Zone.
Choose supported replication or restore procedures.
Verify database and filesystem consistency.
Include recovery time and retained-storage costs.

aws-data/aws-ebs-efs-and-storage-selecti.core: EBS supplies zonal block storage; EFS supplies shared NFS storage with resilience choices. Choose by interface and concurrency semantics, estimate both IOPS and throughput, and verify application-consistent recovery.

storyboard.title: A zonal EBS volume cannot follow arbitrary compute
storyboard.objective: Show the storage constraint during cross-zone recovery.

scenes.title: Normal block access
scenes.caption: Compute uses its compatible zonal volume.
scenes.narration: The database writes through a filesystem or storage engine on an EBS volume in the same Availability Zone.

scenes.title: Compute moves zones
scenes.caption: The original attachment cannot cross the zone boundary.
scenes.narration: A replacement server in another zone cannot simply attach the old zonal volume, so compute redundancy alone is insufficient.

scenes.title: Use a recovery design
scenes.caption: Restoration creates suitable storage in the destination.
scenes.narration: A tested snapshot or replication process provides destination-zone data, followed by consistency checks before the replacement serves traffic.

lesson.title: AWS ElastiCache Redis caching and eviction
lesson.why: Caching can reduce database load until simultaneous misses overwhelm the origin. Correctness and recovery depend on expiry, eviction, invalidation, and replication assumptions.
lesson.what: Design a cache-aside product lookup using ElastiCache-compatible Redis concepts. Treat the database as authoritative and test reasoning with synthetic hit-rate calculations rather than a deployed cache.

concepts.name: Cache-aside separates authority
concepts.body: The application reads the cache, loads a miss from the database, then populates a bounded-lifetime entry. This improves repeated reads but creates an invalidation problem after writes. A cached value should carry enough version or freshness context for the application requirement.

concepts.name: TTL and eviction are different
concepts.body: TTL expires an entry based on time. Eviction removes entries under memory pressure according to the configured policy; noeviction instead makes relevant writes fail when memory is exhausted. Policies considering only expiring keys can behave differently when many entries have no expiry.

concepts.name: Miss storms amplify origin work
concepts.body: If many clients miss the same key together, each may query the database. Request coalescing, bounded concurrency, TTL jitter, and carefully controlled stale serving can reduce pressure. Jitter spreads expiry times but does not repair incorrect invalidation or make stale authorization data safe.

concepts.name: Replication is not absolute durability
concepts.body: Redis-compatible replication and failover behavior depend on the selected engine and deployment. Replication can be asynchronous, so recent acknowledged cache writes may be lost on failover. Keep reconstructible data reconstructible, and do not assume a cache is an authoritative payment ledger.

e2e: Identify data that can tolerate a defined staleness interval and be reconstructed from its source.
Choose cache keys with tenant isolation and versioning where appropriate.
Implement miss loading, bounded TTL, and a write invalidation strategy.
Select memory limits and eviction behavior while monitoring hit rate, evictions, and origin pressure.
Rehearse an empty-cache recovery with load shedding and verify correctness before enabling stale responses.

tasks.name: Choose safe cache data
steps: Compare a public product description with a user's current access revocation state.
Allow a documented short freshness window for the description; require a stricter design for authorization rather than blindly caching both for an hour.

tasks.name: Calculate miss amplification
steps: At 2,000 lookups/second and a 95% hit rate, expected origin demand is 2,000 x 0.05 = 100 reads/second.
After an empty-cache restart, initial misses could approach 2,000/second: twenty times the previous origin load. This model omits coalescing and warmup.

tasks.name: Trace stale refill
steps: Reader A fetches old database value; writer B commits a new value and invalidates the key; A then fills the cache with the old value.
Explain why delete-after-write alone does not eliminate every race. Consider version checks or an explicitly acceptable TTL-bound stale interval.

tasks.name: Plan degraded operation
steps: Design a cache-failure mode with bounded database concurrency, request prioritization, and a circuit breaker for repeated cache errors.
State when stale serving is prohibited. Offline examples do not validate real eviction, failover durability, or IAM behavior.

key_terms: Cache-aside: application-controlled loading after a miss.
TTL: time until an entry becomes expired.
Eviction: removal under memory pressure.
Stampede: concurrent misses causing duplicate origin work.
Hit rate: fraction of lookups served from cache.
lesson.safety: Do not create a cache or use production keys. Real memory capacity, replicas, backups, transfer, and origin overload cost money; never flush a shared cache for practice.
cleanup: Discard synthetic product and key examples.
Future tests must remove their isolated cache and review snapshots rather than flushing unrelated data.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, the database collapses after a healthy cache is restarted. Why can this happen and how would you recover?
interview_points: Calculate the rise in origin demand from cold misses.
Bound concurrency and coalesce repeated key loads.
Warm important keys cautiously and spread expirations.
Preserve correctness and distinguish cache data from authoritative records.

aws-data/aws-elasticache-redis-caching-a.core: Cache-aside needs freshness and invalidation rules. TTL is not eviction; high hit rates conceal cold-cache origin load. Protect the database and never assume replicated cache writes are durable business records.

storyboard.title: Cold Redis cache overloads its database
storyboard.objective: Trace cache misses and controlled recovery.

scenes.title: Warm cache
scenes.caption: Most repeated lookups avoid the database.
scenes.narration: Product requests hit cached entries within their freshness window, keeping authoritative database read demand relatively low.

scenes.title: Cache becomes empty
scenes.caption: Many simultaneous misses expose hidden demand.
scenes.narration: After cache loss, requests reach the database together; previous low database utilization did not represent worst-case demand.

scenes.title: Recover under a bound
scenes.caption: Coalescing and controlled refill protect the origin.
scenes.narration: The application limits concurrent loads, combines repeated key requests, and refills useful entries without promising stale data is always acceptable.

lesson.title: AWS OpenSearch indexing and operations
lesson.why: Search clusters can run out of disk or heap while raw input volume looks modest. Index structure, shard count, replicas, and query patterns determine operational load.
lesson.what: Plan a small log-search domain using explicit mappings, shard budgets, retention, and snapshot recovery. Work from synthetic document sizes rather than indexing real logs.

concepts.name: Mappings define searchable structure
concepts.body: Text fields are analyzed into tokens; keyword fields preserve exact values for filtering and aggregation. Uncontrolled dynamic fields can cause mapping explosion. Choosing analyzers, timestamp formats, and stable field names before ingestion avoids expensive reindexing and inconsistent query results later.

concepts.name: Shards trade parallelism for overhead
concepts.body: An index consists of primary shards, with replicas providing additional copies and read-serving opportunities. Every shard consumes resources, so many tiny shards can waste heap and cluster-management effort. Too few oversized shards can hinder distribution and recovery; there is no universal perfect count.

concepts.name: Ingestion competes with querying
concepts.body: Bulk requests reduce per-request overhead, but oversized batches and excessive concurrency can overload nodes. Refresh controls when indexed changes become searchable; it is not the same as a durable backup. Rejected requests need bounded retry, while sustained queue growth requires capacity or workload changes.

concepts.name: Retention and recovery are operational controls
concepts.body: Index lifecycle or state-management policies can roll over and delete eligible indexes. Disk watermarks can restrict allocation or writes under pressure. Snapshots and restore rehearsals protect recovery needs, while multi-zone placement addresses different failures and does not undo accidental deletion automatically.

e2e: Define searchable fields, expected daily documents, query types, and retention.
Estimate primary data size, replica multiplier, and explicit indexing and free-space overhead.
Choose a starting shard plan and bounded ingestion strategy for representative testing.
Observe disk, heap, latency, rejected work, and shard allocation rather than only node CPU.
Apply reviewed rollover/retention policies and verify snapshot restoration into an isolated target.

tasks.name: Choose field types
steps: For synthetic logs, map message for full-text search and service_name for exact filtering; give event_time a documented date format.
Explain why creating a distinct field name for every request ID is worse than storing IDs as values.

tasks.name: Calculate a storage floor
steps: Assume 12 GB/day of primary indexed data and 14 days retained: 168 GB primary. One replica gives 336 GB before operational overhead.
Add an illustrative 25% planning allowance to get 420 GB. This allowance is an assumption, not an AWS sizing recommendation or tested guarantee.

tasks.name: Diagnose rejected bulk writes
steps: A sample timeline shows ingestion concurrency doubling, write rejections rising, and free disk falling.
Reduce uncontrolled concurrency, inspect disk allocation and heap, and use backoff. Do not conclude that merely increasing retries creates capacity.

tasks.name: Rehearse retention recovery
steps: Propose a snapshot restore check before changing retention from 30 to seven days.
Verify index names, document counts, and representative searches in isolation. Offline arithmetic cannot prove cluster performance, snapshot completeness, or permissions.

key_terms: Mapping: field types and indexing interpretation.
Primary shard: partition of an index's data.
Replica shard: additional shard copy.
Refresh: making recent indexed changes searchable.
Rollover: moving new writes to a new index.
lesson.safety: Do not provision a domain or ingest private logs. Nodes, storage, snapshots, transfer, and retained telemetry can incur costs; logs must be scrubbed of secrets.
cleanup: Future approved tests must account for domains, snapshots, and retained indexes separately before cleanup.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a search cluster has low average CPU but rejects writes. What would you inspect before adding nodes?
interview_points: Inspect disk watermarks, heap, queues, and shard allocation.
Review bulk sizes, concurrency, and retry amplification.
Check mapping growth and excessive shard count.
Validate retention and recovery before deleting data.

aws-data/aws-opensearch-indexing-and-ope.core: OpenSearch sizing starts with mappings, indexed size, replicas, retention, and query behavior. Shards have overhead, refresh is not backup, and retrying rejected writes without controlling load can worsen saturation.

storyboard.title: OpenSearch ingestion reaches a disk constraint
storyboard.objective: Connect retention growth to rejected writes and recovery.

scenes.title: Steady ingestion
scenes.caption: Documents enter indexes with planned mappings.
scenes.narration: The shipper submits bounded batches while index storage grows according to the modeled retention and replica count.

scenes.title: Disk pressure rises
scenes.caption: Rejected work is a capacity signal.
scenes.narration: Retained indexes consume available disk, limiting allocation or writes; immediate repeated retries cannot remove the underlying storage pressure.

scenes.title: Recover with retention evidence
scenes.caption: Protect recovery before removing old indexes.
scenes.narration: Operators validate snapshots, apply reviewed retention, and restore bounded ingestion while watching disk, heap, and rejection metrics.

lesson.title: AWS data migration and database replication
lesson.why: A copied row count does not establish a safe database cutover. Schema compatibility, ongoing changes, lag, business invariants, and the ability to reverse direction determine migration risk.
lesson.what: Plan a DMS-style full-load plus change-data-capture migration between fictional databases. Keep data transport distinct from schema conversion and application compatibility.

concepts.name: Full load seeds a target
concepts.body: A full load copies existing source data according to selected tables and transformations. Source and target engines may differ in types, defaults, generated keys, stored procedures, or collations. Moving rows does not automatically convert every schema object or preserve application semantics.

concepts.name: CDC follows ongoing changes
concepts.body: Change data capture reads supported source change logs and applies changes after initial loading. Correct permissions, log retention, and engine prerequisites are essential. Source and target latency measure different bottlenecks; a lost required log segment can force reseeding rather than a simple retry.

concepts.name: Validation needs multiple layers
concepts.body: Compare counts, key ranges, checksums where meaningful, and business invariants such as account totals. Concurrent writes complicate comparisons, so use a consistent comparison point or understood reconciliation window. Matching counts alone can hide changed values, duplicates, or omitted tables.

concepts.name: Cutover changes the authority
concepts.body: Quiesce or tightly control writes, let replication catch up, validate a final checkpoint, then redirect clients. After the target accepts new writes, rollback is not merely changing a connection string: new target data needs reconciliation or a predesigned reverse-replication strategy.

e2e: Inventory engines, schema objects, application dependencies, and permissible downtime.
Prepare a compatible target and documented source-log and permission prerequisites.
Perform initial loading while retaining enough change history for catch-up.
Monitor lag and validate data at agreed checkpoints using business-level checks.
Fence old writers, complete final reconciliation, switch clients, and retain a time-bounded recovery path.

tasks.name: Inventory incompatibilities
steps: List a table, trigger, stored procedure, sequence, and engine-specific timestamp type.
Mark which require explicit compatibility review rather than assuming a row-copy service converts everything. Add a query-behavior check for the application.

tasks.name: Calculate catch-up time
steps: Assume a backlog of 180,000 changes, target apply capacity of 1,200/second, and continuing source writes of 900/second.
Net catch-up is 300/second, so modeled time is 600 seconds, or ten minutes. If writes rise to 1,300/second, the backlog grows instead; this is not measured service throughput.

tasks.name: Challenge row counts
steps: Source and target each have 100 accounts, but total balances differ by 50 synthetic units.
Reject count-only acceptance. Compare keys and values at a consistent point, then investigate transformations, missed updates, or duplicate application.

tasks.name: Design post-cutover rollback
steps: After cutover, the target receives 200 new orders before an application defect appears.
Explain how to fence writes and preserve/reconcile those orders before returning authority to the source. Offline rehearsal does not prove real DMS compatibility or IAM access.

key_terms: Full load: initial copy of selected data.
CDC: replication driven by database change records.
Replication lag: delay between source change and target application.
Write fencing: preventing competing authoritative writers.
Reconciliation: resolving differences between datasets.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic records only. Migration compute, source load, target storage, logs, and transfer have costs; never enable replication or expose database credentials for this exercise.
cleanup: Keep the cutover and rollback decision gates.
Discard synthetic balances; future migration cleanup must wait for approved retention and source decommissioning decisions.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, replication lag is zero and row counts match. Is it safe to cut over immediately?
interview_points: Check schema and application compatibility.
Validate values and business invariants at a known checkpoint.
Fence old writers and verify client routing.
Plan reconciliation of post-cutover writes before promising rollback.

aws-data/aws-data-migration-and-database.core: Database migration combines initial copy, CDC prerequisites, compatibility work, and business validation. Catch-up requires apply capacity above ongoing writes. Once the target accepts writes, rollback requires preserving that new data.

storyboard.title: CDC catch-up precedes a controlled cutover
storyboard.objective: Show why lag and write authority determine migration safety.

scenes.title: Copy and follow
scenes.caption: Initial data and ongoing changes reach the target.
scenes.narration: The migration worker seeds selected tables and follows retained source logs while the original database remains authoritative.

scenes.title: Apply falls behind
scenes.caption: Incoming changes exceed processing capacity.
scenes.narration: Target apply throughput drops below source write rate, increasing backlog and invalidating the planned cutover time.

scenes.title: Fence and reconcile
scenes.caption: A final checkpoint precedes authority transfer.
scenes.narration: After restoring apply capacity, operators fence old writers, reconcile a final checkpoint, and switch clients with a data-preserving rollback plan.
